rows.stem: Williamson synthesis of preparing unsymmetrical ether is :
rows.solution:
Williamson's synthesis makes an ether by letting a sodium alkoxide attack an alkyl halide, the alkoxide displacing the halide from the back in ONE step.

That is a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution, \(\mathrm{S_N}2\).

Because the step is \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), the halide must be primary: a tertiary halide has too crowded a carbon, and the alkoxide — a strong base as well as a strong nucleophile — eliminates instead, giving an alkene rather than the ether.

rows.stem: Which of the following compounds would be hydrolysed by aqueous KOH most easily ?
rows.solution:
Hydrolysis by aqueous alkali breaks the carbon-halogen bond, so the compound that reacts fastest is the one whose bond is weakest and whose carbocation is best stabilised. That is the ALLYLIC bromide, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH-CH_2-Br}\).

Its halogen sits on the carbon NEXT TO the double bond, so the carbocation left behind is delocalised over two carbons by resonance and is unusually stable.

The vinylic bromide \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH-Br}\) is the opposite case: there the halogen is ON the doubly bonded carbon, its lone pair is fed into the double bond, the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond gains partial double bond character, and it is the hardest of the four to break. The two simple alkyl bromides, primary and secondary, fall in between.

rows.stem: According to Werner’s theory of coordination compounds :

options.label: C
options.text: Both primary and secondary valences are non-ionisable.

options.label: D
options.text: Both primary and secondary valences are ionisable.

rows.solution:
According to Werner, PRIMARY VALENCES ARE IONISABLE.

The primary valence is satisfied by negative ions outside the coordination sphere; those ions dissociate in water and can be precipitated, which is how Werner detected them — silver nitrate precipitates them at once. The secondary valence is satisfied by the ligands attached directly to the metal, and those are held inside the coordination sphere and are non-ionisable.

The primary valence corresponds to what we now call the oxidation state; the secondary valence to the coordination number.

rows.stem: Which of the following complex ion is **not** optically active ?
rows.solution:
The one that is NOT optically active is the TRANS isomer of \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\).

With the two chlorido ligands opposite one another the ion has a plane of symmetry, so it is superimposable on its mirror image and cannot rotate plane polarised light.

The other three have no such plane. The cis form of the same ion is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers, and both \(\mathrm{[Co(ox)_3]^{3-}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) carry three chelate rings arranged like a three bladed propeller, which is chiral for the same reason a screw thread is.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following is the softest metal ?
rows.solution:
ZINC is the softest of the four.

Hardness in these metals tracks the strength of the metallic bonding, which in turn tracks the number of UNPAIRED d electrons available to it. Zinc is \(3d^{10}4s^2\): its d subshell is completely filled, so those electrons take no part in the bonding and only the two \(4s\) electrons do. The interatomic forces are correspondingly weak, and zinc is soft with a low melting point.

Scandium, copper and iron all have d electrons that do participate, so all three are harder.

rows.stem: In the Hinsberg’s method for separation of primary, secondary and tertiary amines, the reagent used is :
rows.solution:
The reagent is BENZENESULPHONYL CHLORIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\), known as Hinsberg's reagent.

It separates the three classes because each responds differently. A primary amine gives a sulphonamide with one hydrogen still on the nitrogen; that hydrogen is acidic, so the product dissolves in alkali. A secondary amine gives a sulphonamide with no hydrogen left on nitrogen, so it stays insoluble in alkali. A tertiary amine has no nitrogen-hydrogen bond to begin with and does not react at all.

Nitrous acid also distinguishes the three, but it is not Hinsberg's reagent; chloroform with alkali is the carbylamine test, which detects primary amines only.

rows.stem: Which one of the following amines gives an alcohol on reaction with \(\mathrm{HNO_2}\) ?
rows.solution:
The amine that gives an ALCOHOL with nitrous acid is the primary ALIPHATIC one, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\).

A primary aliphatic amine forms a diazonium salt that is unstable even at low temperature: it loses nitrogen at once, and the carbocation left behind picks up water, so the isolated product is the alcohol.
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Aniline behaves differently because its diazonium salt is stabilised by the ring and survives at 273-278 K, which is what makes diazotisation synthetically useful. The secondary amine gives an N-nitrosoamine, and the tertiary amine merely forms a salt.

rows.stem: The freezing point of one molal KCl solution, assuming KCl to be completely dissociated in water, is : (\(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water = \(1{\cdot}86\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Potassium chloride is completely dissociated, so each formula unit gives two ions and the van't Hoff factor is \(i = 2\).

\(\Delta T_f = i\,K_f\,m = 2 \times 1{\cdot}86 \times 1 = 3{\cdot}72\) K

Depression is measured DOWN from the freezing point of pure water, which is \(0\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), so the solution freezes at
\(0 - 3{\cdot}72 = -3{\cdot}72\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)

Two traps sit in the options. Forgetting the dissociation gives \(-1{\cdot}86\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), and reading the depression as a temperature rather than a fall gives \(+3{\cdot}72\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\); both are offered.

rows.stem: A solution of acetone in ethanol :

options.label: C
options.text: shows a positive deviation from Raoult’s law.

options.label: D
options.text: shows a negative deviation from Raoult’s law.

rows.solution:
A solution of acetone in ethanol shows a POSITIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law.

Pure ethanol is extensively hydrogen bonded to itself. Adding acetone puts acetone molecules between the ethanol molecules and breaks some of those hydrogen bonds, and acetone cannot replace them in kind — it has no hydrogen on oxygen to donate. The new interactions between unlike molecules are therefore WEAKER than those between like molecules, so the molecules escape more readily than Raoult's law predicts and the observed vapour pressure is higher.

Mixing is endothermic and the volume expands slightly, which is the same fact seen from two other directions.

rows.stem: Which of the following cell converts the energy of combustion of fuel into electrical energy ?
rows.solution:
The FUEL CELL converts the energy of combustion of a fuel directly into electrical energy.

It is a galvanic cell whose reactants are supplied continuously from outside instead of being stored inside it, so it does not run down; the hydrogen-oxygen cell used on the Apollo flights is the standard example.

The other three are all storage devices. Mercury, dry and lead storage cells hold a fixed quantity of reactant sealed inside and are exhausted when it is consumed, although the lead storage cell can be recharged.

rows.stem: The unit of rate and rate constant are same for a :
rows.solution:
Rate and rate constant carry the same units for a ZERO ORDER reaction.

For a reaction of order \(n\) the rate law is \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^n\), so
\(k = \dfrac{\text{Rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]^n}\), with units \(\mathrm{mol^{1-n}\ L^{n-1}\ s^{-1}}\)

The two sets of units agree only when the concentration term disappears, that is when \(n = 0\); there \(k\) has the units of rate itself, \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

For first order the constant is \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), for second order \(\mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) — neither matches the rate.

rows.stem: Pyranose ring of glucose is formed due to the reaction between :
rows.solution:
The pyranose ring is formed between \(\mathrm{C_1}\) AND \(\mathrm{C_5}\).

The hydroxyl group on \(\mathrm{C_5}\) adds across the aldehyde group on \(\mathrm{C_1}\), giving a cyclic hemiacetal. Counting round, that ring contains five carbons and one oxygen — a six membered ring, and it is its resemblance to pyran that gives the name.

The alternative closure, from \(\mathrm{C_4}\), would give a five membered furanose ring; glucose prefers the six membered one, which is why glucose in solution is almost entirely glucopyranose.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Actinoids show wide range of oxidation states.
Reason (R) : Actinoids are radioactive in nature.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Actinoids do show a wide range of oxidation states — uranium alone runs from \(+3\) to \(+6\) — and actinoids are indeed radioactive throughout the series.

But the two facts have different causes. The wide range of oxidation states arises because the \(5f\), \(6d\) and \(7s\) orbitals lie so close in energy that electrons from all three are available for bonding. Radioactivity is a property of the NUCLEUS, not of the valence electrons, and has no bearing on how many electrons an atom can give up.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Hydrolysis of an ester follows first order kinetics.
Reason (R) : The concentration of water does not get altered much during the reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The hydrolysis of an ester genuinely involves two species, the ester and water, so on its stoichiometry it should be second order. It is observed to be first order because water is also the solvent and is present in enormous excess: the fraction of it consumed is negligible, so its concentration stays effectively constant throughout.

That constant concentration is then absorbed into the rate constant, \(\text{Rate} = k'[\text{ester}]\) with \(k' = k[\mathrm{H_2O}]\), and the reaction is first order in practice. This is called a PSEUDO first order reaction, and the Reason states exactly the condition that makes it one.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Boiling point of \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}\) is higher than that of \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\).
Reason (R) : Hydrogen bonding is more extensive in \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

Trimethylamine has no hydrogen on its nitrogen at all, so its molecules cannot hydrogen bond to one another; only weak dipole-dipole forces hold them together. Propan-1-amine is a primary amine with TWO hydrogens on nitrogen, so its molecules associate strongly.

The boiling point therefore runs the other way from the Assertion: propan-1-amine boils HIGHER, at about 321 K, against about 276 K for trimethylamine. The Reason is correct as written, and it is precisely why the Assertion fails.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Phenol is strongly acidic as compared to ethanol.
Reason (R) : Phenoxide ion is more stable than ethoxide ion.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Phenol is the stronger acid, and the reason is what happens to the anion left behind. In the phenoxide ion the negative charge is delocalised into the benzene RING by resonance, spread over the ortho and para carbons as well as the oxygen. In the ethoxide ion the charge has nowhere to go: it sits entirely on one oxygen, and the alkyl group, being electron releasing, pushes still more density onto it.

The more stable the anion, the more readily the parent releases its proton. Phenol has \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 10, ethanol about 16.

rows.stem: State Henry’s law. Why are aquatic species more comfortable in cold water as compared to warm water ?
rows.solution:
HENRY'S LAW. At a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the surface of the liquid. Equivalently, the partial pressure of the gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution:
\(p = K_{\mathrm{H}}\,x\)
where \(K_{\mathrm{H}}\) is the Henry's law constant for that gas in that solvent.

Aquatic species are more comfortable in COLD water because dissolving a gas is an exothermic process, so the solubility of oxygen FALLS as the temperature rises. Warm water therefore holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water at the same pressure, and the species that breathe it are the worse off for it.

This is why thermal pollution — warm water discharged from a power station into a river — threatens fish without adding anything toxic to the water.

rows.stem:
Observe the graph in the given figure and answer the following questions :

(a) Predict the order of reaction.

(b) What is the slope of the curve ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the printed graph is a straight line rising from the origin, y-axis labelled 'log [R]\(_0\) / [R] \(\rightarrow\)' and x-axis labelled 'Time \(\rightarrow\)'. Neither sub-part is answerable without the axis labels; the marking scheme's answers (first order; slope = k/2·303) come straight off them. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) The graph plots \(\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\) against time and comes out a STRAIGHT LINE through the origin. Only one order gives that shape, so the reaction is of FIRST order.

(b) The integrated rate equation for a first order reaction is
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

Rearranged into the form of the plotted line,
\(\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\,t\)

so the slope of the curve is \(\dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\), and it carries no intercept, which is why the line passes through the origin.

Note the sign: had the plot been \(\log[\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\) the line would fall and the slope would be \(-k/2{\cdot}303\). Here the concentration term is inverted, so the line rises and the slope is positive.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following coordination compounds :

(i) \(\mathrm{[CoCl_2(en)_2]SO_4}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{K_3[Fe(C_2O_4)_3]}\)
rows.solution:
(i) The sulphate ion outside the sphere carries \(-2\), so the complex ion is \(+2\). Inside it, two chlorido ligands give \(-2\) and the two ethane-1,2-diamine molecules are neutral, so cobalt must be \(+4\).

Ligands are named alphabetically, chlorido before the diamine, and the bracketed ligand name takes bis- because its own name already contains a numerical prefix:
DICHLORIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)COBALT(IV) SULPHATE

(ii) Here the three potassium ions give \(+3\) and the three oxalato ligands \(-6\), so iron is \(+3\) and the complex is the ANION.

An anionic complex takes the -ate ending on the metal, and for iron that ending is built on the Latin stem: ferrate.
POTASSIUM TRIOXALATOFERRATE(III)

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem:
Differentiate between :

(i) Double salt and Complex compound

(ii) Didentate ligand and Ambidentate ligand
rows.solution:
(i) A DOUBLE SALT exists only in the solid state. Dissolve it and it dissociates completely into the same simple ions as its two parent salts, so a solution of carnallite, \(\mathrm{KCl \cdot MgCl_2 \cdot 6H_2O}\), gives the ordinary tests for potassium, magnesium and chloride.

A COMPLEX COMPOUND does not. Its coordination sphere survives dissolution, so the complex ion goes into solution intact and the species inside it give no independent test. Potassium hexacyanidoferrate(II) in water gives no test for iron(II), because the iron never becomes a free ion.

(ii) A DIDENTATE ligand binds the metal through TWO donor atoms AT THE SAME TIME, closing a ring around it — ethane-1,2-diamine uses both its nitrogens, the oxalate ion two of its oxygens.

An AMBIDENTATE ligand has two different donor atoms but binds through only ONE of them at a time, and the choice of which gives rise to linkage isomerism. The nitrite ion may attach through nitrogen, as nitro, or through oxygen, as nitrito; the thiocyanate ion through sulphur or through nitrogen.

The distinction is between binding through two atoms at once and having a choice of two atoms to bind through.

rows.stem:
Draw the structures of major monohalo products in each of the following reactions :

(a) 1-Methylcyclohex-1-ene + HI \(\longrightarrow\) ?

(b) Cyclohexene + \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) \(\xrightarrow{\text{Heat or UV light}}\) ?
rows.solution:
(a) 1-Methylcyclohex-1-ene with hydrogen iodide is an electrophilic ADDITION, and it follows Markovnikov's rule: the proton adds to the doubly bonded carbon that already carries more hydrogens, so the iodide goes to the carbon bearing the methyl group.

That carbon then holds both a methyl group and an iodine, and it is a TERTIARY centre — which is exactly why the reaction takes this course, the tertiary carbocation being the more stable intermediate.

Product: 1-iodo-1-methylcyclohexane, a cyclohexane ring with \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{I}\) on the SAME carbon.

(b) Cyclohexene with bromine under heat or ultraviolet light is not an addition at all. Those conditions generate bromine RADICALS, and a radical abstracts a hydrogen rather than adding to the double bond. It takes the one it can abstract most easily, which is the ALLYLIC hydrogen on the carbon next to the double bond, because the radical left behind is delocalised over the double bond.

Product: 3-bromocyclohexene, the ring keeping its double bond with \(\mathrm{Br}\) on the adjacent carbon.

The contrast between the two parts is the point of the question: bromine water in the dark would add across the double bond to give the 1,2-dibromide, but that is a DIhalo product, and the question asks for monohalo.

rows.stem:
How do you explain the following ?

(a) Presence of an aldehydic group in glucose.

(b) Presence of five – OH groups in glucose.
rows.solution:
(a) Treat glucose with a MILD oxidising agent — bromine water. It oxidises glucose to a six carbon carboxylic acid, gluconic acid. Bromine water is too mild to attack a hydroxyl group, so the only thing in the molecule it can have oxidised is an ALDEHYDE group, and its presence is thereby established.
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}\text{ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)

(b) Treat glucose with ACETIC ANHYDRIDE. Acetylation gives glucose PENTAacetate — five acetyl groups go on, and each one requires a hydroxyl group to attach to. Five acetyl groups therefore mean FIVE hydroxyl groups in the molecule.
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)

The two experiments together account for six of the seven carbons' worth of functional groups, and each proves its point by counting rather than by inspection.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Vapour pressure of pure water at 298 K is \(24{\cdot}8\) mm Hg. Calculate the lowering in vapour pressure of an aqueous solution which freezes at \(- 0{\cdot}3\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). (\(\mathrm{K_f}\) of water = \(1{\cdot}86\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
The freezing point tells us the molality, and the molality tells us the mole fraction of the solute; the lowering of vapour pressure follows from that.

Step 1 — molality from the depression. The solution freezes at \(-0{\cdot}3\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), so \(\Delta T_f = 0{\cdot}3\) K:
\(m = \dfrac{\Delta T_f}{K_f} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}3}{1{\cdot}86} = 0{\cdot}161\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Step 2 — mole fraction of the solute. Molality counts moles of solute per kilogram of water, and a kilogram of water is \(1000/18\) moles. The solution is dilute, so the solute may be neglected in the denominator:
\(x_2 = \dfrac{m \times 18}{1000} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}161 \times 18}{1000} = 2{\cdot}90 \times 10^{-3}\)

Step 3 — lowering of vapour pressure. By Raoult's law the RELATIVE lowering equals the mole fraction of the solute:
\(\dfrac{p_1^{\,\circ} - p_1}{p_1^{\,\circ}} = x_2\)
so the lowering itself is
\(p_1^{\,\circ} - p_1 = x_2\,p_1^{\,\circ} = 2{\cdot}90 \times 10^{-3} \times 24{\cdot}8\)

Lowering in vapour pressure \(= 0{\cdot}07\) mm Hg

The question asks for the LOWERING, not the vapour pressure of the solution; that would be \(24{\cdot}8 - 0{\cdot}07 = 24{\cdot}73\) mm Hg.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate of a reaction :

A + B \(\longrightarrow\) product

is given below as a function of different initial concentrations of A and B.

| Experiment | [A] / mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) | [B] / mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) | Initial Rate/mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\,min^{-1}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | \(0{\cdot}01\) | \(0{\cdot}01\) | \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) |
| 2 | \(0{\cdot}02\) | \(0{\cdot}01\) | \(1 \times 10^{-2}\) |
| 3 | \(0{\cdot}01\) | \(0{\cdot}02\) | \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) |

Calculate the order of the reaction with respect to A and B. Determine the rate constant of the reaction.
rows.solution:
Compare the experiments in PAIRS, changing one concentration at a time.

Order with respect to \(\mathrm{B}\). Between experiments 1 and 3, \([\mathrm{B}]\) doubles from \(0{\cdot}01\) to \(0{\cdot}02\) while \([\mathrm{A}]\) is held at \(0{\cdot}01\). The rate does not move — it is \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) both times:
\(\dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{5 \times 10^{-3}} = \left(\dfrac{0{\cdot}02}{0{\cdot}01}\right)^{q}\), so \(1 = 2^{q}\) and \(q = 0\)

Order with respect to \(\mathrm{A}\). Between experiments 1 and 2, \([\mathrm{A}]\) doubles while \([\mathrm{B}]\) is held fixed, and the rate doubles from \(5 \times 10^{-3}\) to \(1 \times 10^{-2}\):
\(2 = 2^{p}\), so \(p = 1\)

Order with respect to \(\mathrm{A}\) is 1; with respect to \(\mathrm{B}\) is 0. The overall order is 1.

Rate constant, from experiment 1 and the rate law \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]\):
\(5 \times 10^{-3} = k \times 0{\cdot}01\)
\(k = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

The unit is a check on the work: a first order constant must come out as reciprocal time, and it does.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :

(a) The pH of aqueous NaCl increases when it is electrolysed.

(b) Unlike dry cell, mercury cell has a constant cell potential through its lifetime.

(c) Conductivity of solution decreases with dilution.
rows.solution:
(a) Electrolysing aqueous sodium chloride does not discharge sodium at the cathode — water is reduced in preference, because its reduction potential is far less negative:
\(2\mathrm{H_2O} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2} + 2\mathrm{OH^-}\)
Hydroxide ions accumulate in the solution, and with the sodium ions already present the product is sodium hydroxide. More hydroxide means a less acidic solution, so the pH RISES.

(b) The potential of a cell falls as it runs whenever the overall reaction changes the concentration of an ion in the solution, because the Nernst term then shifts. The mercury cell is built so that it does not: its overall reaction, zinc with mercury(II) oxide giving zinc oxide and mercury, involves no ion in solution at all — every species in it is a solid. With nothing in the Nernst quotient to change, the potential stays at about \(1{\cdot}35\) V throughout the cell's life.

The dry cell is the contrast: its reaction produces and consumes ions in the paste, so its voltage falls steadily as it is used.

(c) Conductivity is the conductance of a solution held between electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre — it is a property of a fixed VOLUME. Diluting the solution puts fewer ions in that volume, so fewer charge carriers are available between the electrodes and the conductivity falls.

Molar conductivity behaves the opposite way, RISING on dilution, because it counts the ions from a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte rather than a fixed volume, and dilution lets those ions dissociate and move more freely.

rows.stem:
Answer the following about the complexes \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\) and \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) :

(i) Write the hybridization involved in each case.

(ii) Which of them is the outer orbital complex and which one is the inner orbital complex ?

(iii) Compare their magnetic behaviour.

[Atomic number : Fe = 26]
rows.solution:
Iron is atomic number 26, so the neutral atom is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^6 4s^2\).

In \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\) the six fluorides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-3\), so iron is \(+3\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) is \(3d^5\).
In \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) the six cyanides give \(-6\) against an overall \(-4\), so iron is \(+2\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\).

(i) Hybridisation. Fluoride is a WEAK field ligand and cannot force the five \(3d\) electrons to pair, so no inner \(3d\) orbital is left vacant and bonding must reach outwards to the \(4d\) set: \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\) is \(sp^3d^2\).
Cyanide is a STRONG field ligand and pairs the six \(3d\) electrons into the three \(t_{2g}\) orbitals, freeing two inner \(3d\) orbitals: \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) is \(d^2sp^3\).

(ii) The names follow directly from which d orbitals were used. \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\), using the outer \(4d\), is the OUTER ORBITAL complex; \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\), using the inner \(3d\), is the INNER ORBITAL complex.

(iii) Magnetic behaviour follows from the pairing. \(\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}\) keeps all five electrons unpaired and is strongly PARAMAGNETIC, with \(\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = 5{\cdot}92\) B.M. \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}}\) has all six paired and is DIAMAGNETIC, \(\mu = 0\).

rows.stem:
(i) What happens to the colour of complex \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) when heated gradually ?

(ii) Write the electronic configuration for \(\mathrm{d^5}\) ion if \(\Delta_\mathrm{o} <\) P.

(iii) Write the hybridization and magnetic behaviour of the complex \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\).

[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
rows.solution:
(i) The colour of \(\mathrm{[Ti(H_2O)_6]^{3+}}\) FADES AWAY, and the solution finally becomes colourless.

The violet colour comes from a d-d transition: the single \(3d\) electron of \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) absorbs light and jumps from the \(t_{2g}\) set to the \(e_g\) set. Heating drives off the water ligands, and once the ligands are gone there is no crystal field, no splitting, and no transition left to absorb light.

(ii) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\) means the splitting costs LESS than pairing, so electrons spread out singly over all five orbitals before any pair up. For \(d^5\) that gives the HIGH SPIN arrangement:
\(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^2\)
with five unpaired electrons. Had \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} > \mathrm{P}\) the configuration would have been \(t_{2g}^5\,e_g^0\), with one.

(iii) Nickel is atomic number 28, and in \(\mathrm{[Ni(CO)_4]}\) it is in the ZERO oxidation state, \(3d^8 4s^2\). Carbon monoxide drives the two \(4s\) electrons into the \(3d\) set, giving \(3d^{10}\) — completely filled, with no \(3d\) orbital free. Bonding must therefore use the \(4s\) and all three \(4p\) orbitals.

Hybridisation \(sp^3\), so the geometry is tetrahedral; with no unpaired electron the complex is DIAMAGNETIC.

rows.stem:
Write any two differences between \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reactions. Which of the following compounds would undergo \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction faster and why ?

\(\mathrm{C_6H_{11} - CH_2 - Cl}\)  or  \(\mathrm{C_6H_5 - CH_2 - Cl}\)
rows.solution:
Two differences between the two substitution routes:

MOLECULARITY. \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) is unimolecular — only the substrate appears in the rate determining step, so the kinetics are first order and the rate does not depend on the nucleophile's concentration at all. \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) is bimolecular, substrate and nucleophile both in the one step, so the kinetics are second order and the rate depends on both.

STEREOCHEMISTRY. \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) goes through a planar carbocation, which the nucleophile can attack from either face, so an optically active substrate gives a RACEMIC mixture. \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) has the nucleophile attack from the side opposite the leaving group in a single step, so the configuration is INVERTED.

A third difference, if one is wanted: \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) passes through a carbocation intermediate and is favoured by polar protic solvents, while \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) passes through a transition state with no intermediate and is favoured by polar aprotic ones.

Which reacts faster by \(\mathrm{S_N}1\): BENZYL CHLORIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH_2-Cl}\).

Since the rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set by how easily the carbocation forms, the question is which cation is the more stable. The benzyl cation is stabilised by RESONANCE — its positive charge is delocalised into the benzene ring, over the ortho and para positions. The cyclohexylmethyl cation from \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-CH_2-Cl}\) has a saturated ring beside it and no such delocalisation; it remains a plain primary carbocation.

rows.stem: A compound (A) with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_5N}\) on reduction with DIBAL-H followed by hydrolysis, gives a compound (B). Compound (B) gives positive Tollens’ test but does not give iodoform test. Compound (B) can also be obtained when ethanal is treated with dilute NaOH followed by heating. Identify (A) and (B). Write the reactions of (A) with DIBAL-H followed by hydrolysis.
rows.solution:
Work backwards from compound \(\mathrm{B}\), which is the better described of the two.

Compound \(\mathrm{B}\) gives a positive Tollens' test, so it is an ALDEHYDE. It does not give the iodoform test, so it carries no methyl group on the carbonyl carbon. And it is also obtained from ethanal with dilute alkali followed by heating — that is the aldol condensation, two molecules of ethanal joining and then losing water:
\(2\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCHO} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCHO}\), but-2-enal

Compound \(\mathrm{A}\) is then whatever gives that aldehyde with DIBAL-H followed by hydrolysis. DIBAL-H is a partial reducing agent: it takes a NITRILE only as far as the imine, and hydrolysis of the imine gives the aldehyde. So \(\mathrm{A}\) is the nitrile with the same carbon skeleton:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCN}\), but-2-enenitrile

The molecular formula confirms it. \(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCN}\) counts as \(\mathrm{C_4H_5N}\), exactly as stated.

The reaction asked for:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCN} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_2O}]{1.\ \text{DIBAL-H}} \mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCHO}\)

Note that DIBAL-H leaves the carbon-carbon double bond untouched, which is why the but-2-ene skeleton survives the reduction intact.

rows.stem:
How will you obtain the following from aniline ? Give chemical equations only.

(a) Sulphanilic acid

(b) Phenylisocyanide

(c) Acetanilide
rows.solution:
(a) SULPHANILIC ACID. Aniline first forms its salt with sulphuric acid, and heating that salt to 453-473 K rearranges it so the sulphonic acid group ends up on the ring at the para position:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}H_3\,HSO_4^{-}} \xrightarrow{453\text{-}473\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{p\text{-}H_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}SO_3H}\)

(b) PHENYL ISOCYANIDE, by the carbylamine reaction. Chloroform with alcoholic potassium hydroxide generates dichlorocarbene, which a primary amine attacks; the foul smell of the product is the test's signature:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

(c) ACETANILIDE, by acetylation with acetic anhydride. Pyridine is added to mop up the acetic acid released, which would otherwise protonate the amine and stop the reaction:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} \xrightarrow{\text{pyridine}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

rows.stem:
What happens when phenol is treated with the following ?

(i) \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water

(ii) Conc. \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
rows.context: Alcohols undergo a number of reactions involving the cleavage of C – OH bond. However, phenols do not undergo reactions involving the cleavage of C – OH bond. Alcohols are weaker acids than water. Alcohols react with halogen acids to form the corresponding haloalkanes. Phenols are stronger acids than alcohols. A characteristic feature of phenols is that they undergo electrophilic substitution reactions such as halogenation, nitration, etc. Since – OH group is a strong activating group, phenol gives trisubstituted products during halogenation, nitration, etc.
rows.solution:
(i) With BROMINE WATER, phenol gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-TRIBROMOPHENOL.

All three available positions are substituted at once, and no catalyst is needed. The hydroxyl group is so strongly activating — its lone pair is fed into the ring, raising the electron density most at the ortho and para positions — that even the feeble electrophile present in bromine water suffices.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3OH} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

(ii) With CONCENTRATED NITRIC ACID, phenol gives 2,4,6-TRINITROPHENOL, better known as picric acid.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{C_6H_2(NO_2)_3OH}\)

Dilute nitric acid stops at the mono-substituted stage, giving a mixture of 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol; it is the concentrated acid that carries the substitution all the way round.

rows.stem: Write the mechanism of alcohol reacting as nucleophile in a reaction with \(\mathrm{CH_3^{\oplus}}\).
rows.context: Alcohols undergo a number of reactions involving the cleavage of C – OH bond. However, phenols do not undergo reactions involving the cleavage of C – OH bond. Alcohols are weaker acids than water. Alcohols react with halogen acids to form the corresponding haloalkanes. Phenols are stronger acids than alcohols. A characteristic feature of phenols is that they undergo electrophilic substitution reactions such as halogenation, nitration, etc. Since – OH group is a strong activating group, phenol gives trisubstituted products during halogenation, nitration, etc.
rows.solution:
The alcohol acts as a nucleophile through the LONE PAIR on its oxygen, and the mechanism has two steps.

Step 1 — the oxygen's lone pair attacks the carbocation, forming a bond and leaving the oxygen positively charged as a protonated ether:
\(\mathrm{R{-}\ddot{O}{-}H} + \mathrm{\overset{+}{C}H_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}\overset{+}{O}(H){-}CH_3}\)

Step 2 — the oxygen sheds the proton it no longer has room for, giving the neutral ether:
\(\mathrm{R{-}\overset{+}{O}(H){-}CH_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

The whole of the alcohol's nucleophilic character sits in that lone pair, which is why the oxygen, not the hydroxyl hydrogen, is what moves first.

rows.stem: Why do phenols not undergo reactions involving cleavage of C – OH bond ?
rows.context: Alcohols undergo a number of reactions involving the cleavage of C – OH bond. However, phenols do not undergo reactions involving the cleavage of C – OH bond. Alcohols are weaker acids than water. Alcohols react with halogen acids to form the corresponding haloalkanes. Phenols are stronger acids than alcohols. A characteristic feature of phenols is that they undergo electrophilic substitution reactions such as halogenation, nitration, etc. Since – OH group is a strong activating group, phenol gives trisubstituted products during halogenation, nitration, etc.
rows.solution:
Because in a phenol the \(\mathrm{C-OH}\) bond is far stronger than it is in an alcohol, for two reasons that reinforce each other.

The carbon carrying the hydroxyl group is \(sp^2\) hybridised, not \(sp^3\). An \(sp^2\) carbon has more s character, holds its bonding electrons closer to the nucleus, and forms a shorter, stronger bond.

And the oxygen's lone pair is delocalised into the RING by resonance, which gives the \(\mathrm{C-OH}\) bond partial DOUBLE BOND character. A bond with double bond character does not break to let a nucleophile substitute for the hydroxyl group.

The same delocalisation that makes phenol a stronger ACID than an alcohol therefore makes it unreactive towards the substitutions an alcohol undergoes readily. Breaking the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond is made easier; breaking the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond is made harder.

rows.stem: How can you distinguish between Butan-1-ol and 2-Methylpropan-2-ol by using HCl in the presence of anhydrous \(\mathrm{ZnCl_2}\) ?
rows.context: Alcohols undergo a number of reactions involving the cleavage of C – OH bond. However, phenols do not undergo reactions involving the cleavage of C – OH bond. Alcohols are weaker acids than water. Alcohols react with halogen acids to form the corresponding haloalkanes. Phenols are stronger acids than alcohols. A characteristic feature of phenols is that they undergo electrophilic substitution reactions such as halogenation, nitration, etc. Since – OH group is a strong activating group, phenol gives trisubstituted products during halogenation, nitration, etc.
rows.solution:
This is the LUCAS TEST. Add the Lucas reagent — concentrated hydrochloric acid with anhydrous zinc chloride — to each alcohol at room temperature and watch for cloudiness, which is the insoluble chloroalkane separating out.

2-METHYLPROPAN-2-OL gives TURBIDITY IMMEDIATELY. It is a tertiary alcohol, so it reacts by the unimolecular route through a tertiary carbocation, which forms fast.

BUTAN-1-OL gives NO turbidity at room temperature. It is a primary alcohol; it would have to react by the bimolecular route, and that needs heating.

A secondary alcohol, had one been offered, would sit between the two and turn cloudy in about five minutes — which is what makes the test a three way one.

rows.stem:
Define the following :

(i) Peptide linkage

(ii) Denatured protein
rows.context: The \(\alpha\)-amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. All \(\alpha\)-amino acids exist as zwitter ion due to which they show amphoteric behaviour. All amino acids are joined through peptide bond. Proteins are broadly classified as globular proteins and fibrous proteins. Globular proteins are water soluble, whereas fibrous proteins are not. The complete structure of protein is discussed at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures. Protein loses its biological activity in denatured form.
rows.solution:
(i) PEPTIDE LINKAGE. The amide linkage, \(-\mathrm{CO-NH}-\), that joins two amino acids: the carboxyl group of one condenses with the amino group of the next, a molecule of water is lost, and the bond formed between the carbon and the nitrogen is the peptide linkage.

(ii) DENATURED PROTEIN. A protein whose native structure has been destroyed by a physical change such as heating, or a chemical one such as a change in pH, so that it has LOST ITS BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY.

The weak forces holding the chain in shape are disrupted, so the helix uncoils and the globule unfolds: the secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed while the primary structure, the sequence of residues, survives intact — no peptide bond is broken. Boiling an egg is the everyday instance.

rows.stem: Why do amino acids show amphoteric behaviour ?
rows.context: The \(\alpha\)-amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. All \(\alpha\)-amino acids exist as zwitter ion due to which they show amphoteric behaviour. All amino acids are joined through peptide bond. Proteins are broadly classified as globular proteins and fibrous proteins. Globular proteins are water soluble, whereas fibrous proteins are not. The complete structure of protein is discussed at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures. Protein loses its biological activity in denatured form.
rows.solution:
Because an amino acid in the solid state and in solution exists as a ZWITTER ION.

The carboxyl group is acidic enough to lose its proton and the amino group basic enough to take it, so the proton transfers WITHIN the molecule: the carboxyl becomes \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\) and the amino becomes \(-\mathrm{\overset{+}{N}H_3}\), leaving a species with both a positive and a negative centre and no net charge.

That ion can then react in either direction. Facing an acid, the carboxylate end accepts a proton; facing a base, the ammonium end gives one up. Having a group ready for each is what amphoteric behaviour means.

rows.stem: How can you differentiate between Fibrous protein and Globular protein ?
rows.context: The \(\alpha\)-amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. All \(\alpha\)-amino acids exist as zwitter ion due to which they show amphoteric behaviour. All amino acids are joined through peptide bond. Proteins are broadly classified as globular proteins and fibrous proteins. Globular proteins are water soluble, whereas fibrous proteins are not. The complete structure of protein is discussed at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures. Protein loses its biological activity in denatured form.
rows.solution:
The difference is in the SHAPE of the polypeptide chain, and the solubility follows from it.

A FIBROUS protein has its chains running PARALLEL to one another, held side by side by hydrogen bonds and disulphide bridges, giving a long thread-like structure. It is INSOLUBLE in water. Keratin in hair and nail, and myosin in muscle, are fibrous.

A GLOBULAR protein has its chain coiled and folded back on itself into a roughly SPHERICAL shape, with the water-repelling side chains tucked inside and the water-attracting ones on the surface. It is SOLUBLE in water. Insulin and albumin are globular.

The functions follow from the shapes: fibrous proteins are structural material, globular ones the enzymes and hormones.

rows.stem: Write the names of two different secondary structures of proteins.
rows.context: The \(\alpha\)-amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. All \(\alpha\)-amino acids exist as zwitter ion due to which they show amphoteric behaviour. All amino acids are joined through peptide bond. Proteins are broadly classified as globular proteins and fibrous proteins. Globular proteins are water soluble, whereas fibrous proteins are not. The complete structure of protein is discussed at four different levels i.e. primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structures. Protein loses its biological activity in denatured form.
rows.solution:
The two secondary structures of proteins are the \(\alpha\)-HELIX and the \(\beta\)-PLEATED SHEET.

Both are held in shape by hydrogen bonds between the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) of one peptide linkage and the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) of another. In the \(\alpha\)-helix the chain coils like a spring and the hydrogen bonds run within the same chain; in the \(\beta\)-pleated sheet the chains are stretched out side by side and the hydrogen bonds run between neighbouring stretches.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate \(\mathrm{E_{cell}}\) of a galvanic cell in which the following reaction takes place at \(25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) :

\(\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Pb^{2+}}(0{\cdot}02\ \mathrm{M}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) + \mathrm{Pb(s)}\)

[Given : \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}} = - 0{\cdot}76\) V, \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Pb^{2+}/Pb}} = - 0{\cdot}13\) V; \(\log 2 = 0{\cdot}3010\), \(\log 4 = 0{\cdot}6021\), \(\log 5 = 0{\cdot}6990\)].

(ii) State Faraday’s first law of electrolysis. How much electricity, in terms of Faraday, is required to reduce one mol of \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ion ?
rows.solution:
(i) The reaction as written has zinc oxidised and lead deposited, so zinc is the anode and lead the cathode — consistent with zinc's being the more negative of the two potentials.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}} = (-0{\cdot}13) - (-0{\cdot}76) = 0{\cdot}63\ \mathrm{V}\)

Two electrons are transferred, so \(n = 2\), and the reaction quotient uses the two concentrations given:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}]}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}63 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{0{\cdot}02}\)
\(= 0{\cdot}63 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times \log 5\)
\(= 0{\cdot}63 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times 0{\cdot}6990\)
\(= 0{\cdot}63 - 0{\cdot}0206\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}61\ \mathrm{V}\)

The correction is small and NEGATIVE because the product ion is at the higher concentration, which pushes the reaction slightly the wrong way. The solid zinc and solid lead do not enter the quotient at all.

(ii) FARADAY'S FIRST LAW OF ELECTROLYSIS. The amount of chemical reaction occurring at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.

For the reduction asked about, find the change in oxidation state. In \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}}\) the four oxides give \(-8\) against an overall \(-1\), so manganese is \(+7\); in \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) it is \(+2\). Each manganese therefore gains FIVE electrons:
\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\mathrm{H^+} + 5e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}\)

One mole of permanganate needs 5 mol of electrons, that is 5 FARADAY.

rows.stem:
(i) The resistance of a conductivity cell containing \(0{\cdot}001\) M KCl solution at 298 K is 1000 ohm. What is the cell constant if conductivity of \(0{\cdot}001\) M KCl solution at 298 K is \(0{\cdot}125 \times 10^{-3}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) ?

(ii) Calculate the \(\mathrm{E_{Mg^{2+}/Mg}}\) potential for the following half cell at \(25\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) :

\(\mathrm{Mg/Mg^{2+}}\) (\(1 \times 10^{-4}\) M); \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{Mg^{2+}/Mg}} = + 2{\cdot}36\) V

[Given : \(\log 10 = 1\)]

(iii) What is the effect of temperature on the electrical conductance of metallic conductor ?
rows.solution:
(i) Conductivity and conductance are related through the cell constant, \(\kappa = G^{*} \times \dfrac{1}{R}\), so
\(G^{*} = \kappa \times R\)
\(= 0{\cdot}125 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}} \times 1000\ \Omega\)

Cell constant \(G^{*} = 0{\cdot}125\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

The units confirm the arithmetic: siemens and ohm cancel one another, leaving reciprocal centimetres, which is what a cell constant must be — it is the electrode separation divided by the electrode area.

(ii) A single electrode potential obeys the Nernst equation in the same form as a whole cell, with the metal ion in the denominator:
\(E_{\mathrm{Mg^{2+}/Mg}} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Mg^{2+}/Mg}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}]}\)
\(= 2{\cdot}36 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{1}{10^{-4}}\)
\(= 2{\cdot}36 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times 4\log 10\)
\(= 2{\cdot}36 - 0{\cdot}118\)

\(E_{\mathrm{Mg^{2+}/Mg}} = 2{\cdot}242\ \mathrm{V}\)

Take the standard value from the question as it is printed rather than from memory: most data books tabulate the magnesium couple at \(-2{\cdot}36\) V, and the paper supplies \(+2{\cdot}36\) V. The arithmetic above uses the figure given; with the tabulated sign the same working returns \(-2{\cdot}478\) V. Either way the CORRECTION is \(0{\cdot}118\) V and it is subtracted, because a metal ion below unit concentration makes the electrode a poorer oxidising agent.

(iii) The electrical conductance of a METALLIC conductor DECREASES as the temperature rises.

Current in a metal is carried by electrons moving through a lattice of positive ions. Heating makes those ions vibrate more violently, the electrons collide with them more often, and the resistance rises. An electrolytic solution behaves the opposite way, its conductance rising with temperature because the ions themselves move faster and the solvent thins.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
(i) Account for the following :

(I) Orange colour of \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) ion changes to yellow when treated with an alkali.

(II) Zn, Cd and Hg are non-transition elements.

(III) \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}}\) value for \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}\) couple is highly positive (\(+1{\cdot}57\) V) as compared to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr^{2+}}\).

(ii) What happens when :

(I) Manganate ion undergoes disproportionation reaction in acidic medium ?

(II) \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) is heated ?
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Because the dichromate is converted to CHROMATE. In alkali the equilibrium
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
is driven to the right, and it is the chromate ion that is yellow while the dichromate is orange. Acidifying reverses the change and the orange returns, so the interconversion is a pH-controlled equilibrium, not a redox change — chromium stays at \(+6\) throughout.

(II) Because zinc, cadmium and mercury have COMPLETELY FILLED d orbitals both in the ground state and in their common oxidation states. Each is \(d^{10}s^2\) as the atom and \(d^{10}\) as the \(+2\) ion. A transition element is defined as one with a partly filled d subshell in at least one of its stable states, and none of these three ever has one — which is why they lack the characteristic transition metal properties of colour, variable oxidation state and catalytic activity.

(I I I) Because the two couples are reducing to ions of very different stability. \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^5\), an exactly HALF-FILLED subshell and therefore unusually stable, so manganese(III) is strongly inclined to be reduced to it and the potential is large and positive.

\(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), on the other hand, is \(3d^3\), which in an octahedral field is the stable half-filled \(t_{2g}^3\) arrangement — so it is chromium(III) that is the settled species here, and there is little driving force to reduce it to \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\). The chromium potential is accordingly small and negative.

(ii)(I) Manganate disproportionates in acid, the same element being oxidised and reduced at once: some manganese goes from \(+6\) up to \(+7\) as permanganate, the rest down to \(+4\) as manganese dioxide. The green solution turns purple:
\(3\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

(II) Heating potassium permanganate decomposes it to potassium manganate, manganese dioxide and oxygen — again manganese ending in two different oxidation states, \(+6\) and \(+4\):
\(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :

(i) What is ‘Misch metal’ ? Give its one use.

(ii) Write the formula of an oxoanion of chromium in which it shows the oxidation state equal to its group number.

(iii) Why does Vanadium pentoxide (\(\mathrm{V_2O_5}\)) act as a catalyst ?

(iv) Why do transition elements have high enthalpies of atomisation ?

(v) How do you prepare \(\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7}\) from \(\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\) ?
rows.solution:
(i) MISCH METAL is an alloy of a lanthanoid with iron — roughly 95% lanthanoid and 5% iron, with traces of sulphur, carbon, calcium and aluminium.

Its use: it is pyrophoric, so it is used in making BULLETS AND SHELLS and as the flint of a cigarette lighter.

(ii) Chromium is in group 6, so the oxoanion wanted is one in which chromium is in the \(+6\) state:
\(\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}\), the chromate ion

Check the arithmetic: four oxides give \(-8\) against an overall \(-2\), so chromium is \(+6\). The dichromate ion \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) serves equally well, its two chromiums being \(+6\) apiece.

(iii) Because vanadium shows VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES. In the Contact process vanadium(V) oxide hands oxygen to sulphur dioxide and drops to vanadium(IV), then takes oxygen back from the air and returns to vanadium(V). Moving between two accessible states and returning to the original one is exactly what a catalyst must do — it offers the reaction a lower-energy path and is itself unchanged at the end.

(iv) Because transition metals have a LARGE NUMBER OF UNPAIRED ELECTRONS in their atoms, and those electrons take part in the metallic bonding.

More unpaired electrons mean stronger interatomic interaction — stronger metallic bonding — and enthalpy of atomisation measures precisely the energy needed to pull those atoms apart into a gas. The series peaks in the middle, where the unpaired electrons are most numerous, and falls away at zinc, where the d subshell is full and none is available.

(v) By ACIDIFYING the sodium chromate solution. Adding acid shifts the chromate-dichromate equilibrium to the dichromate side, and the orange sodium dichromate crystallises out on concentration:
\(2\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

rows.stem:
(i) Identify A, B and C in the following reactions :

Toluene \(+\ \mathrm{CrO_3}\ \xrightarrow[273 - 283\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}}\) A \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3O^{+}}}\) B, and B \(\xrightarrow{\text{Conc. NaOH}}\) C + sodium benzoate

(ii) Give reasons for the following :

(I) Carboxylic acids do not give the characteristic reactions of carbonyl group.

(II) Ethanoic acid is a stronger acid than ethanol.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — Sub-part (i) is printed as a BRANCHED two-dimensional reaction scheme with DRAWN structures: toluene is a skeletal benzene ring bearing CH3 (not written as a formula), the horizontal chain runs toluene -> A -> B, and a separate arrow drops VERTICALLY from B, labelled 'Conc. NaOH', to a line reading 'C +' followed by a drawn benzene ring bearing COONa. rows.solution:
(i) Toluene with chromium trioxide in acetic anhydride at 273-283 K undergoes a CONTROLLED oxidation of its methyl group. The anhydride protects the product as a DIACETATE, which is what stops the oxidation going all the way to the acid:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CH(OCOCH_3)_2}\), benzylidene diacetate

Hydrolysis with acid removes the two acetate groups and unmasks the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\), benzaldehyde

Benzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen, so with concentrated alkali it cannot undergo aldol and undergoes the CANNIZZARO reaction instead: one molecule oxidises the other. The named product is sodium benzoate, so the partner is the alcohol:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH}\), benzyl alcohol

(ii)(I) Because the carbon of the carboxyl group is much LESS ELECTROPHILIC than that of an aldehyde or ketone. The hydroxyl oxygen donates a lone pair to it by resonance, so the carbon carries far less positive charge than a plain carbonyl carbon does, and a nucleophile has little to attack.

The characteristic carbonyl reactions — addition of hydrogen cyanide, of bisulphite, of ammonia derivatives — all begin with a nucleophile attacking that carbon, so none of them proceeds.

(II) Because the anion left behind is the more stable of the two. When ethanoic acid gives up its proton, the negative charge on the ETHANOATE ion is delocalised by resonance over TWO equivalent oxygen atoms, both electronegative and both sharing it equally.

The ethoxide ion from ethanol has no such escape: the charge is stuck on a single oxygen, and the ethyl group pushes more electron density onto it. The more stable the anion, the more readily the proton leaves — so ethanoic acid, with \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 4.76, is enormously the stronger of the two.

(i) Write the product(s) in the following reactions :

(I) \(2\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}}\)

(II) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + \mathrm{(CH_3)_2Cd} \rightarrow\)

(III) Benzene-1,2-dicarboxamide \(\xrightarrow{\text{strong heating}}\)

(ii) Write the reaction involved in the following reactions :

(I) Wolff-Kishner Reduction

(II) Decarboxylation Reaction
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Phosphorus pentoxide is a dehydrating agent: it pulls a molecule of water out from between two molecules of the acid, leaving the ANHYDRIDE:
\(2\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}} (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
The product is ethanoic anhydride.

(II) A dialkylcadmium is a mild alkylating agent — mild enough to stop at the KETONE instead of attacking it further, which is why it is preferred to a Grignard reagent here:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl} + (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Cd} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\)
The product is acetophenone.

(I I I) Strong heating of benzene-1,2-dicarboxamide drives ammonia out from between the two amide groups, closing a five-membered ring:
benzene-1,2-dicarboxamide \(\xrightarrow{\text{strong heating}}\) PHTHALIMIDE
a ring bearing \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\), \(\mathrm{NH}\) and \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) fused to the benzene ring.

(ii)(I) WOLFF-KISHNER REDUCTION converts a carbonyl group all the way to \(\mathrm{CH_2}\), in two stages. Hydrazine first condenses with it to the hydrazone, and heating that with a strong base then expels nitrogen:
\(\mathrm{C{=}O} \xrightarrow[-\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{NH_2NH_2}} \mathrm{C{=}N-NH_2} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{KOH}/\text{ethylene glycol}} \mathrm{CH_2} + \mathrm{N_2}\)
It is the alkaline counterpart of Clemmensen reduction, which achieves the same conversion in acid.

(II) DECARBOXYLATION removes the carboxyl group as carbonate, leaving a hydrocarbon with one carbon fewer. The sodium salt of the acid is heated with soda lime, that is sodium hydroxide with calcium oxide:
\(\mathrm{R-COONa} \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\mathrm{NaOH}\ \text{and}\ \mathrm{CaO}} \mathrm{R-H} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)
